name: Interview behavioural questions, set 3
description: Spoken behavioural questions with model answers and rubrics. Topics: disagreement, missing information, a failing team, learning, strengths, being stumped, CV lines and estimates. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Describe a time you disagreed with someone more senior than you. What did you do, and how did it end?
widget.model: Last summer I disagreed with my supervisor about how to test a pricing model. I was an intern on a small analytics team. She wanted to report the model's error on the full year of data. I thought the last two months had a different pattern, so one average would hide it. I did not argue in the meeting. Instead I split the data by month that afternoon and made one chart. The error was 2% for ten months and 9% for the last two. I sent her the chart with a short note and asked for ten minutes. She agreed the split mattered, and we reported both numbers. The team then added a monthly check to every model review. I learned to bring evidence, not opinions, to a senior person. I also learned to raise it privately first, so nobody has to back down in public.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: who was senior and what the disagreement was about
A specific situation: the setting, your role and what was at stake
Your own actions in the first person, including how you raised it
Evidence or a number, and how the disagreement ended
A lesson about disagreeing with someone senior, stated plainly
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer shows you can disagree with respect and with evidence. Name the point of disagreement early, then spend most of the time on what you did. End with the outcome, even if you turned out to be wrong.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Tell me about a decision you had to make without all the information you wanted.
widget.model: In my final year I had to choose a dataset for my dissertation with only a week to decide. I was modelling how news affects share prices. One source covered ten years but had gaps. The other was clean but covered only three years. My proposal was due on Friday, and nobody could tell me whether the clean set would grow. I listed what I knew and what I did not. Then I tested both sets on one simple question in two days. The long set gave the same answer as the clean one once I dropped the gappy months. That cost me 15% of the rows but kept seven years of extra history. I chose it, wrote down the assumption, and set a check for the gaps. The final model held up under my supervisor's tests. Now I decide with what I have, and I write down what would change my mind.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: the decision and what was missing
A specific situation: the deadline, the options and the stakes
Your own actions: what you checked, what you assumed and why
A number or concrete result from the decision
What new information would have changed the choice
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer separates what you knew from what you assumed. It shows a quick, cheap test before committing, and a decision made on time. Saying what would change your mind shows you held the decision loosely.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Describe a time you worked in a team that was failing. What did you do?
widget.model: In my second year our four-person team was failing a group coding project. We were building a timetable app, and with two weeks left nothing ran end to end. Two people had written large parts that did not fit together. Meetings had turned into blame. I suggested we stop adding features for three days. I drew the data flow on one page and asked each person to own one link. I took the part nobody wanted, the tests between the pieces. We met for fifteen minutes each morning and said only what was blocked. By the end of the first week the app ran end to end. We cut two features and handed in a working app on time. We scored 68%, up from a predicted fail at the midpoint review. I learned that a failing team often needs a smaller goal, not more effort.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: the team, the task and how it was failing
A specific situation: the deadline and what was at stake
Your own actions in the first person, not only what the team did
A number or concrete result after the change
A lesson about teams, stated plainly
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer says how the team was failing in one sentence, then what you did about it. Keep "we" for the team and "I" for your own part, so the interviewer can see your role. Describe the problem, not the people, and blame nobody.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: What would you want to learn in your first six months on a trading desk?
widget.model: In my first six months I would want to learn three things, in order. First, the products and the risk we run on them: what moves our P&L, and why. I would ask to sit with the risk report every morning until I could explain each line. Second, the desk's tools and its rules. I would aim to quote a simple product on my own within three months, under supervision. Third, how good traders think under pressure. I would keep a notebook of each mistake I see, mine included, and what fixed it. In a society trading game last year I kept such a log. After twenty sessions my average loss on a bad trade fell by about a third. On a desk I would expect that log to teach me more than any course. By month six I would want my mentor to trust me with a small book.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence with a clear structure, such as three things
Shows the substance of the job: risk, products, quoting or the desk's tools
Specific actions you would take to learn, not only topics
Evidence from your past with a number, such as a log or a game
A goal for the end of the six months
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer shows you know what the job involves and how you learn. Give a short structure, then a concrete action for each part. Back it with one past example, so the plan sounds tested rather than hoped for.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: In two minutes, describe your biggest strength and give one example of it.
widget.model: My biggest strength is checking my own work before others rely on it. Last year I ran the scoring for a student trading competition with forty teams. Each round, teams sent trades by form, and I turned them into scores. In the first round my spreadsheet ranked one team third. Something looked off, because their trades were small. I rebuilt their score by hand from the raw forms. A formula had summed one column twice, and three teams were affected. I fixed it before the results went out, so nobody saw a wrong table. After that I added a check that compared each total with a hand count for two random teams. Across six rounds that check caught two more errors. The competition finished with no disputed scores. I bring the same habit to coding and to data work.

rubric.text: Names the strength in the first sentence
One specific example: when, what, and what was at stake
Your own actions in the first person
A number or concrete result that shows the strength
Links the strength to the role in one line
Within two minutes, at a steady pace, ending with a clear last sentence

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A recorded answer is marked for a clear structure in a short time. Name one strength, prove it with one story, and close by linking it to the job. Practise to a timer, because two minutes passes quickly.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: You are in the final round and a question stumps you. Talk me through what you do in the next minute.
widget.model: First, I say so calmly, and I restate the question to check I have it right. Say it is a probability puzzle I cannot see a route through. I would say, "I do not see the trick yet, so let me try a small case." Then I shrink it: two players instead of ten, or one roll instead of five. I work the small case aloud, because the interviewer marks the reasoning. If a pattern appears, I say what I expect and test one more case. If I am still stuck after a minute, I say what I would try next. I might ask whether a nearby idea, such as symmetry, points the right way. In a mock last term this turned a blank into a partial answer worth most of the marks. I would rather show a clear process than sit in silence.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: owns the block and restates the question
Names a concrete method, such as a small case or a simpler version
Reasons aloud in the first person, step by step
A specific example, or a clear next step when still stuck
Asks a useful clarifying question, not for the answer
Calm, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: Interviewers expect you to get stuck and mark what you do next. Say so, restate the problem, and try a smaller case aloud. Asking a precise question is fine; asking for the answer is not.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Pick the weakest line on your CV and defend it.
widget.model: The weakest line on my CV is "Member, investment society." On its own it says nothing about what I did. Here is what sits behind it. In my second year the society ran a paper portfolio of £10,000 in pretend money. I joined the four-person team that wrote the weekly market note. I wrote eight of the twenty notes, each under a page. I also built the spreadsheet that tracked the portfolio against an index. It showed we lagged the index by 3% over the term, mostly from fees we had ignored. We changed our rule to trade less often, and the gap halved the next term. So the line is weak as written, and I will rewrite it. It should say: "Wrote 8 weekly market notes; built a tracker that halved our gap to the index."

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: names one weak line honestly
Says why it is weak and what sits behind it
Your own actions in the first person, with specifics
A number or concrete result that the line could show
Says how you would rewrite the line
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: Interviewers ask this to see whether you can judge your own work honestly. Pick a real weak line, say what it hides, and give the evidence behind it. Ending with a better version of the line shows you can take feedback.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Estimate aloud how many cups of coffee are sold in the United Kingdom each day. Then tell me what would change your mind. You have two minutes.
widget.model: I will build it from people, not shops. The UK has about 67 million people. Say 60% are adults who drink hot drinks, about 40 million. I would guess half of those drink coffee on a given day, so 20 million. A coffee drinker has about two cups, so 40 million cups a day. Many of those are made at home, not bought. If a quarter are bought, that is about 10 million sold cups. So my estimate is 40 million cups drunk, and around 10 million sold. My weakest input is the share bought. I would check it against the number of coffee shops. If there are 30,000, my figure means about 330 cups each a day. That feels high for a small café, so I might lower the bought share. A survey of daily coffee habits would change my mind fastest.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence with a plan for the estimate
Breaks the number into stated inputs with round values
Reasons aloud in the first person, one step at a time
Gives a number and checks it by a second route
Names the weakest input and the data that would change the answer
Within two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer states a plan, then builds the number from a few round inputs said aloud. A second route, such as counting shops, checks the result. Naming the weakest input and the data that would fix it answers the follow-up.
